blocks.text: Proof of Theorem. Remainder theorem on "Complex polynomials" (Algebra · /algebra/complex-numbers/complex-polynomials#proof-1)

Proof:
Polynomial division gives

$$
p(z)=(z-\alpha)q(z)+r,
$$

with a constant remainder $r$. At $z=\alpha$, the first term vanishes, leaving $p(\alpha)=r$.
- Theorem. Remainder theorem: When $p(z)$ is divided by $z-\alpha$, the remainder is the complex number $p(\alpha)$.

- Definition. Polynomial root: A number $\alpha\in\mathbb C$ is a *root* of $p$ if

$$
p(\alpha)=0.
$$

- Definition. Complex polynomial: A *complex polynomial* is a function $p:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ of the form

$$
p(z)=a_0+a_1z+a_2z^2+\cdots+a_nz^n,
\qquad a_0,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb C,
$$

for a non-negative integer $n$.

- Definition. Complex number: A *complex number* is a number of the form

$$
z=a+bi,\qquad a,b\in\mathbb R,\qquad i^2=-1.
$$

The expression $a+bi$ is the Cartesian form of $z$. Its real part is $\operatorname{Re}(z)=a$ and its imaginary part is $\operatorname{Im}(z)=b$.
